The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments are the operative regime as of 2 Jan 2023.

* Electronic monitoring – ESA s.37.1/37.2. In force 1 Jan 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25+ employees. Written policy required on that date and provision to employees; an employer that first reaches 25+ after 1 Jan 2022 has 3 months to comply.
* Disconnecting from work – ESA s.43.1/43.2. In force 2 June 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25+ employees. Written policy required on that date and provision to employees; an employer that first reaches 25+ after the effective date has 6 months to comply.

Triggering is assessed on the 1 Jan 2022 / 2 June 2022 / 1 July 2022 reference headcount. Once the 25+ threshold is met on the reference date the policy duty attaches for that year; a later fall below 25 is debated.

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023 → 28 later. <25 on both trigger dates, no statutory disconnect/electronic monitoring duty as of 2 Jan 2023. Grace period only starts 10 Jan 2023. Compliant.

B – 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates so no statutory duty to have a disconnect or electronic monitoring policy. The employer has voluntary policies since 2020/2021. Majority view: refusal to distribute voluntary policies is not a statutory breach because the statutory duty to have/distribute is not engaged. Minority view: if the policies exist the ESA provision/communication duty attaches and a blanket refusal to give them to new hires is non-compliance; the same minority also notes a possible 20-employee disconnect phase-in from 1 Jan 2023.

C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and throughout 2022, i.e. >25 on all trigger dates. Written and “appropriately distributed” disconnect and electronic monitoring policies are in place. Debate on the monthly update / quarterly distribution practice: the ESA requires a copy of the policy on hire and a copy of any change to the policy to be provided to employees. Updating monthly but only circulating a copy every fiscal quarter means employees can be up to ~2-3 months out of date. Majority view in the main stream is that this is de facto compliance; a minority argues this is a failure to give an updated policy promptly and therefore non-compliant.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. The 25+ threshold is met on the 1 Jan 2022 reference date for electronic monitoring and on the 2 June 2022 reference date for disconnecting. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy but has never developed an electronic monitoring policy. Headcount falls to 24 on 15 Mar 2022 and stays at 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Main stream: the electronic monitoring obligation was triggered by the 30-employee count on 1 Jan 2022 and was required to be in place by 1 Jan 2022. The subsequent drop below 25 does not retroactively cure the failure to ever have the policy; the employer remains without the required electronic monitoring policy as of 2 Jan 2023. This is the classic “once triggered” breach identified by most colleagues. Minority “current headcount” view would say the employer is now <25 and therefore no policy is currently required.

E – 22 employees on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after the 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 give 24. <25 on both trigger dates and on 2 Jan 2023. No statutory disconnect/electronic monitoring duty as of the assessment date. Compliant.

Unresolved points: the exact effect of a post-trigger headcount drop on the continuing duty; the timeliness requirement for providing changed policies in C; and the possible 20-employee disconnect phase-in effective 1 Jan 2023 raised by some colleagues which would make A, B and E more problematic.

Current best synthesis: the clear historic statutory failure is D’s absence of an electronic monitoring policy where the 25+ threshold was met on 1 Jan 2022. C’s quarterly distribution of monthly changes is the strongest alternative current-headcount non-compliance argument.
reflection_text.1:
Round 0 discussion has been about the Ontario ESA Working for Workers amendments as they stand on 2 Jan 2023.

Legal baseline repeatedly cited:
* Electronic monitoring written policy – ESA s.78.1ff. In force 1 Jan 2022 for employers who regularly employ 25+ employees. Triggered by 25+ on the statutory reference date; 3-month grace on first crossing.
* Disconnecting from work written policy – ESA s.43.1ff. In force 2 June 2022 for 25+; Working for Workers Act 2022 lowers the disconnect threshold to 20+ employees with effect 1 Jan 2023. Duty to have written policy and to provide it to employees, and to provide a copy of any revised policy when changed.

Head-count analysis that keeps recurring:
A. 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 → 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. Under a 25+ test no disconnect/e-m policy is required on 2 Jan 2023 – the 3/6-month clock would only start 10 Jan 2023. Under a 20+ disconnect test as of 1 Jan 2023 the employer is at the threshold on 2 Jan 2023 and has no disconnect policy at all.
B. 23 employees on assessment date. <25 so e-m policy not statutorily required. With a 20+ disconnect test a disconnect policy is required; employer has a written disconnect policy since 2020 and an e-m policy since late 2021 but refuses to distribute either to new hires on cost grounds. Distribution obligation is in issue.
C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 range. Clearly >25/20 on all material dates. Has written and “appropriately distributed” disconnect and e-m policies. Fact pattern: policies updated every month but a copy is provided to each employee only every fiscal quarter. Dispute over whether that quarterly provision satisfies the “provide a copy of any new/revised policy” duty. Some colleagues read it as timely, others as a failure to provide the update contemporaneously with a change.
D. 30 employees 1 Jan 2022 → 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and on 2 Jan 2023. Has a written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, has never developed an e-m policy. Under a strict 25+ reference-date/once-triggered view the e-m obligation attached on 1 Jan 2022 and the subsequent fall to 24 does not cure the historic absence of an e-m policy. Under a current-headcount view the employer is <25 on 2 Jan 2023 so e-m is not required; disconnect is required under the 20+ test and the employer does have a disconnect policy.
E. 22 employees 1 Jan 2022 → -2 Aug 2022 → -2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 take headcount to 24. <20 on 2 Jan 2023 and <25 for e-m. No statutory policy required on the assessment date.

Majority public stance in round 0 is D as the historic e-m breach for an employer that was 30 strong on 1 Jan 2022 and never put an e-m policy in place. Arguments for D stress once-triggered coverage and that the March 2022 reduction does not retroactively extinguish the 1 Jan 2022 e-m obligation.

A significant minority pushes C on the policy-update/distribution timeliness point: monthly changes with quarterly distribution is not “providing the updated policy” as required by ss.43.1/43.2.

A further minority pushes B on distribution refusal, and a few colleagues, Colleague 15/18, highlight the 1 Jan 2023 20-employee disconnect expansion, which would make A the clearest current non-compliance for want of any disconnect policy with 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023, and would also make B’s refusal to distribute a disconnect policy a statutory breach.

Unresolved tensions:
* Is the disconnect threshold for 2 Jan 2023 still 25+ or already 20+? The 20+ amendment changes A, B and E analysis.
* Is the e-m/disconnect obligation head-count locked on the statutory reference date and “once triggered always required”, or is it assessed on current headcount on 2 Jan 2023?
* What is the legally sufficient timing for providing a revised policy – is quarterly provision after monthly changes a breach or merely sub-optimal practice?

My current understanding is that the 20+ disconnect expansion effective 1 Jan 2023 is decisive. On that reading A is non-compliant for having no disconnect policy with 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023, B is also non-compliant for refusing to provide a required disconnect policy to new hires, and C’s quarterly distribution of monthly updates is at least arguable non-compliance. The classic 25+ once-triggered reading that makes D the answer remains the dominant colleague consensus and is the historic teaching point for e-m.
reflection_text.8:
The deliberation is about the two Working for Workers Act, 2021 written-policy duties under the ESA and the head-count trigger dates.

* Electronic monitoring: 25+ employees, in force 1 Jan 2022 / compliance 11 Mar 2022. 
* Disconnecting from work: 25+ employees, in force 2 Jun / 1 Jul 2022. From 1 Jan 2023 the disconnect duty is lowered to 20+ employees, with a number of colleagues noting a possible 6-month phase-in for the 20-24 band. The trigger is generally taken as the head-count on the statutory reference date, 1 Jan 2022 for the 2022 year, and ongoing size for 2023.

Current head-counts on 2 Jan 2023:

A. 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023, 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 for electronic monitoring. On a strict 20+ disconnect reading as of 1 Jan 2023 the employer is covered and has no disconnect policy. Some colleagues argue a grace period runs from 10 Jan 2023 when the 25+ threshold is first crossed; others treat the 20+ duty as immediate.

B. 23 employees. Has written disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021 but refuses to distribute to new hires on cost grounds. <25 so electronic monitoring not statutorily required. With 23 employees the disconnect duty is engaged under the 20+ rule, and the ESA requires the policy to be provided to employees, including new hires. Refusal to distribute is therefore a distribution breach if the duty is treated as engaged; if a grace period applies the breach is the distribution failure rather than lack of policy.

C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, >25 at all material times. Has written and “appropriately distributed” both policies. Updates policies monthly but only gives employees a copy every fiscal quarter. The ESA requires a revised policy to be provided to employees when it changes. A monthly change with quarterly provision is a timely-provision argument. Several colleagues read this as non-compliance; others read quarterly issue as sufficient in substance.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and on 2 Jan 2023. Has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. The electronic monitoring duty was triggered by the 30-employee count on 1 Jan 2022 and was in force for 2022. A majority of colleagues treat the 1 Jan 2022 trigger as locking in the duty for the year and hold that the subsequent drop to 24 does not cure the historic failure to have a written electronic monitoring policy. On a pure current-head-count reading the employer is <25 on 2 Jan 2023 so neither duty is presently required, and the disconnect policy is supererogatory.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug resignations → 18 after 31 Dec retirements. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023, 24 after 15 Feb 2023 hires. <25 for electronic monitoring and, on a 20+ reading, <20 on 2 Jan 2023. No policy required on the assessment date.

Unresolved points affecting the choice: whether the 20+ disconnect expansion is immediate on 1 Jan 2023 or has a 6-month grace period; whether a triggered electronic monitoring duty continues after the head-count falls below 25; and whether a monthly-updated / quarterly-distributed policy satisfies the “provide on change” obligation. The most persistent classic breach discussed is D’s absence of a required electronic monitoring policy for a 30-employee employer on 1 Jan 2022, with C’s delayed update of a required policy and B’s refusal to distribute a voluntarily held policy as the main competing current breaches, and A’s lack of a disconnect policy under the new 20+ threshold as a further candidate if the threshold is immediate.
reflection_text.18:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA create two written-policy duties.

* Electronic monitoring s.37.1/37.2 etc.: in force 1 Jan 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25+ employees. Trigger is the 1 Jan 2022 headcount for the year; an employer who first reaches 25+ later has a 3 month grace period.
* Disconnecting from work s.43.1/43.2 etc.: in force 1 Jul 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25+ employees. Trigger is the 1 Jan/1 Jul headcount; an employer who first reaches 25+ later has a 6 month grace period. There is also discussion in the round about the Working for Workers 2022 phase-in lowering the disconnect threshold to 20+ from 1 Jan 2023, which would change the analysis for A/B/E.

Headcount snapshots relevant to 2 Jan 2023:

* A: 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and through 2022, still 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates, so no statutory electronic monitoring or disconnecting policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. On a 20+ disconnect threshold from 1 Jan 2023 the employer would be caught for disconnect absent a policy, and the 8 hires would trigger the 25+ duties from 10 Jan 2023.
* B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on the 1 Jan 2022 and 1 Jul 2022 trigger dates, so neither duty is statutorily required. The employer voluntarily has both policies since 2020/2021. Refusal to distribute to new hires is not a statutory breach on a strict 25+ reading; it would be a breach of the provision/distribution duty if the 20+ disconnect threshold applies from 1 Jan 2023 and the employer is in fact required to maintain/provide the policy.
* C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and throughout 2022, always >25. Statutorily required to have both a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic monitoring policy, and to have provided them to employees. Employer says both are written and appropriately distributed. The contested point is the monthly update / quarterly distribution practice. The ESA requires a copy of any new or revised policy to be provided to employees; providing an updated policy up to ~90 days after a monthly change is argued by some colleagues as untimely provision, and by others as a reasonable method of keeping employees advised. That is the present-day distribution-timing argument.
* D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, then 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees for remainder of 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. Disconnecting policy is written and appropriately distributed; electronic monitoring policy is never developed. The 30-employee headcount on 1 Jan 2022 triggers the electronic monitoring duty for 2022, and the duty was in force 1 Jan 2022. The subsequent fall to 24 does not retroactively cure the failure to have a written electronic monitoring policy in place when the 25+ threshold was met on the statutory reference date. On a current-headcount reading the employer is now <25 and the disconnect duty would not be engaged for 2023, but the historic trigger remains the classic breach. This is the position taken by the majority of colleagues.
* E: 22 employees 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 = 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 bring headcount to 24. <25 on both trigger dates and on 2 Jan 2023, so no statutory policy is required. Under a 20+ disconnect threshold from 1 Jan 2023 the employer remains below threshold.

Unresolved/tension points from the round:
* Whether the 25-employee test is a one-year snapshot tied to 1 Jan 2022 or a rolling “regularly employs” test that disappears once headcount falls below 25. Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,16,21,4,5,7 argue the obligation once triggered is not cured by a later reduction; colleagues 11,20,3,6 argue compliance should be assessed on current 2 Jan 2023 headcount.
* The effect of the Working for Workers 2022 phase-in to 20+ employees for disconnect from 1 Jan 2023, raised by colleagues 15,18. If that phase-in is accepted, A would be non-compliant for lacking a disconnect policy with 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023, and B’s refusal to distribute a required disconnect policy would be a breach.
* The C distribution-timing issue: whether “provide a copy of the updated policy” requires contemporaneous distribution on change or permits quarterly batching of monthly changes. Colleagues 11,20,3,6 treat this as a clear breach; colleagues 1,10,12,4 treat it as substantive compliance.

Current best synthesis: On the classic 25+ trigger-date teaching used in the question, D is the clear statutory failure – an employer who was 30 strong on 1 Jan 2022 and therefore required to have a written electronic monitoring policy from 1 Jan 2022, who never developed one, while maintaining a disconnect policy. C’s quarterly distribution of monthly policy updates is a plausible alternative breach, and B’s refusal to distribute becomes relevant only if the 20+ disconnect threshold from 1 Jan 2023 is applied. The majority view in round 0 points to D as the employer not in compliance as of 2 January 2023.
reflection_text.12:
The discussion is focused on the Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA and the head-count trigger dates.

* Electronic monitoring – in force 1 Jan 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25+ employees. A written policy must be in place and provided to employees; an employer who first reaches 25+ later has a 3 month grace period.
* Disconnecting from work – in force 2 Jun / 1 Jul 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25+ employees. A written policy must be in place and provided to employees; an employer who first reaches 25+ later has a 6 month grace period.

Several colleagues note a further amendment that lowers the disconnect threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, and one colleague reads it as a 1+ employer rule from 1 Jan 2023. That is the main source of divergence.

On a classic 25+ snapshot interpretation:

* A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023, 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates, no statutory disconnect/electronic-monitoring duty as of 2 Jan 2023. The 28-person level will only be reached after 10 Jan 2023.
* B – 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates so no statutory duty to have a disconnect or electronic-monitoring policy. The policies are voluntary; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not a statutory breach under a strict 25+ reading, although distribution is required if a policy is maintained.
* C – ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, >25 on 1 Jan 2022 / 1 Jul 2022 / 1 Jan 2023. Written disconnect and electronic-monitoring policies exist and are said to be appropriately distributed. Arguable issue is the monthly update / quarterly distribution practice: s.43.1/43.2 requires a copy of a new or revised policy to be provided to employees when it changes. Updating monthly but only circulating quarterly is raised as a late provision of revised policies.
* D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees for remainder of 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. The electronic-monitoring duty was triggered by the 1 Jan 2022 30-person headcount. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy but has never developed an electronic-monitoring policy. Headcount falling to 24 does not cure the failure to have the electronic-monitoring policy in place at the time the obligation attached, and the policy is still absent on 2 Jan 2023. This is the historic non-compliance most colleagues point to.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 Aug 2022, –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <25 on the relevant dates, no statutory policy duty as of 2 Jan 2023.

Under the 25+ reading the clearest statutory failure is D’s absence of a required electronic-monitoring policy for the period it was a 25+ employer, even though its current headcount is 24.

If the 20+ disconnect threshold effective 1 Jan 2023 is applied, the analysis shifts:
* A would now be caught: 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023 with no disconnect policy, so a breach of the 20+ disconnect duty.
* B would be caught on distribution: 23 employees ≥20, a disconnect policy is required and the employer does have one, but a blanket refusal to distribute it to new hires is a failure of the provision obligation.
* E remains <20 on 2 Jan 2023.
The monthly-update/quarterly-distribution issue for C remains a live alternative non-compliance argument.

Unresolved points: whether the disconnect threshold is 25 or 20/1 on 2 Jan 2023, whether an obligation triggered on a reference date persists after headcount falls below the threshold, and whether monthly policy changes with quarterly circulation satisfies the “provide a copy of any new or revised policy” duty. The majority of colleagues currently converge on D as the employer not in compliance.
reflection_text.6:
The threshold regime under the Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA is central.

Electronic monitoring – s. 43.1/43.2 ESA. In force 1 Jan 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25+ employees. A written policy must exist and be provided to employees, with an update provided on change. First compliance date / grace is 3 months on first crossing the threshold.

Disconnecting from work – s. 50.1/50.2 ESA. In force 2 June 2022 for 25+ employees. First compliance date / grace is 3 months on first crossing the threshold. Working for Workers 2022 then lowers the disconnect threshold to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, with 1-19 employees following 1 Jan 2024. Colleagues are split on whether that 20+ phase-in is to be applied on the 2 Jan 2023 assessment date.

Head-count snapshot vs current head-count:
* A: 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 and through 2022; 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023 → 28. Under a strict 25+ test no policy is yet required on 2 Jan 2023 and a 3/6 month grace would run from 10 Jan 2023. Under the 20+ disconnect phase-in effective 1 Jan 2023, a 20-person employer is now captured for disconnecting and has no written disconnect policy – a clear current breach. The facts are clearly drafted to test a post-2 Jan 2023 grace period.
* B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. Under 25+ test no statutory disconnect/electronic monitoring duty arises; the existing voluntary policies can be kept but distribution is not statutorily mandated. Under 20+ disconnect phase-in the employer is now captured for disconnecting, it does have a written disconnect policy since 2020 and an online monitoring policy since 2021, but it refuses to distribute the policies to new employees on cost grounds. The ESA provision duty attaches once a policy is required, so refusal to provide it to new hires is a distribution breach. Colleagues disagree whether a voluntary policy creates a distribution duty.
* C: ~1,000 employees 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Clearly >25 on both trigger dates for electronic monitoring and disconnecting. Employer states written and appropriately distributed both policies. Issue raised by several colleagues is the provision of updates: policies are updated monthly but a copy is only given to each employee every fiscal quarter. ESA requires a copy of any new or revised policy to be given to employees; monthly change with quarterly delivery can be up to ~90 days late. Some colleagues read that as non-compliance with the “provide on change” obligation, others read quarterly circulation as substantively compliant.
* D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. Electronic monitoring obligation triggered 1 Jan 2022; disconnecting obligation triggered on the June/July 2022 effective date. Six employees terminated 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees for remainder of 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. Employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy but “has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring”. Under a once-triggered reading the electronic monitoring duty attached on 1 Jan 2022 when the employer was 30 strong and the absence of a written electronic monitoring policy is a continuing statutory breach even after headcount falls below 25. Under a current-headcount reading the employer is now <25 and the electronic monitoring duty is no longer active for 2023, and the disconnect policy it holds is supererogatory. This is the classic persistence-of-obligation point and is the answer most colleagues converge on.
* E: 22 employees 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 → 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24. Under 25+ test no policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. Under 20+ disconnect phase-in the employer is below 20 on 2 Jan 2023, so still no disconnect duty; the 24-employee headcount only arrives after the assessment date.

Unresolved / contentious points:
- Whether the 20+ disconnect phase-in effective 1 Jan 2023 is to be applied on 2 Jan 2023. If it is, A and B become captured for disconnecting and A is missing a policy, B is failing distribution.
- Whether a policy obligation, once triggered by the 1 Jan 2022/1 July 2022 snapshot, persists after the employer falls below 25 employees. Most colleagues treat it as persisting for the year and D is non-compliant for lacking an electronic monitoring policy.
- The timeliness of policy updates for C: monthly revision vs quarterly distribution. A minority view treats this as a breach of s.43.1/43.2 provision-on-change duties; majority treats it as substantively compliant.

Current working synthesis: On the classic 25+ trigger-date teaching that dominates the round-0 discussion, the clearest statutory failure is D’s absence of a required electronic monitoring policy for an employer who was 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and never put the policy in place. That is the historic non-compliance that remains visible on 2 Jan 2023. The 20+ disconnect expansion and C’s update-distribution timing remain live alternative readings that could make A/B/C also appear non-compliant under a strict current-date reading.
reflection_text.3:
The round-0 discussion is split mainly on D vs C, with a minority B position.

Threshold and timing that colleagues agree on:
* Electronic monitoring policy – ESA s.78.1 ff., in force 1 Jan 2022 for employers who regularly employ 25+ employees; disconnecting from work – ESA s.43.1 ff., in force 1 Jul 2022 / 2 Jun 2022 for employers who regularly employ 25+ employees. The statutory size test is normally taken on the reference date 1 Jan 2022 and thereafter on the date the obligation comes into force. Once the 25-employee threshold is met on the reference date an employer must have a written policy in place and provide it to employees; a first-time crossing after the reference date gives a 3-month / 6-month grace period.

Application to the facts:
* A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements that start 10 Jan 2023 will only take the employer to 28 in the future. <25 on both trigger dates, no disconnecting/electronic monitoring duty as of 2 Jan 2023. Compliant.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 bring the employer to 24. Never 25+ on the material dates. No policy required. Compliant.
* B – 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates so no statutory duty to have a disconnecting-from-work or electronic-monitoring policy. The employer has voluntary policies since 2020/2021. The refusal to distribute them to new hires is a cost defence and is not a statutory breach where the duty to have the policies is not engaged. Most colleagues treat B as compliant; a minority treats the refusal to provide voluntarily adopted policies as a distribution breach.
* C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022, >25 on both 1 Jan 2022 and 1 Jul 2022. Statutorily required to have both a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy and to provide them. The facts state the policies are written and “appropriately distributed”. The contested point is the monthly update vs quarterly provision: updating every month but only giving a copy to each employee every fiscal quarter. Several colleagues argue that is a late provision of a revised policy, i.e. a failure of s.43.1/43.2 to give a copy of a new/revised policy when it is changed, and therefore C is the current-headcount non-compliant employer. Others treat quarterly re-issue as substantively compliant.

* D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 triggers the 25+ class for the 2022 year. An electronic-monitoring policy was required on the 1 Jan 2022 effective date and a disconnecting-from-work policy was required when the disconnect obligation came into force. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy but has never developed an electronic-monitoring policy. Headcount falls to 24 on 15 Mar 2022 and stays at 24 through 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023.

Majority view in round 0: the 1 Jan 2022 headcount of 30 triggers the electronic-monitoring duty and the duty is not cured by the later fall to 24. The absence of a required electronic-monitoring policy for an employer who was 30 strong on the statutory reference date is a continuing non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023. That is the classic trigger-date breach illustrated by D.

Minority/current-headcount view: once the employer is <25 on 2 Jan 2023 the 2023 obligation no longer applies, so D is now compliant and the only clear current non-compliance is C’s failure to provide revised policies contemporaneously with the monthly changes, i.e. the monthly update / quarterly distribution practice.

Unresolved / needing to lock down: whether the ESA obligation is assessed on a “once triggered, remains triggered for the year” basis or on a pure current-headcount basis as of 2 Jan 2023; the exact timing requirement for providing a revised policy; and the effect, if any, of the Working for Workers 2022 phase-in to 20+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, which some colleagues raised. On the classic 25-employee trigger-date analysis the consensus non-compliant employer is D for lack of a required electronic-monitoring policy.
reflection_text.10:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 creates two written-policy duties under the ESA for employers who regularly employ 25 or more employees: 
* electronic monitoring – in force 1 Jan 2022; 
* disconnecting from work – in force 1 Jul 2022 / 2 Jun 2022. 

The duties are triggered by the head-count on the statutory reference date and, on the dominant reading in the room, once triggered the requirement is not retroactively cured by a later down-turn in numbers; the policy must exist in writing and be provided to employees, and any revised policy must be provided promptly on change.

* A – 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023 now sits on the 20-employee disconnect threshold that took effect 1 Jan 2023 under the Working for Workers Act, 2022. On a strict immediate-trigger reading the employer needs a disconnect policy now and has none, though many colleagues treat the 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 as the future trigger and give a 3/6-month grace period. <25 on the 1 Jan 2022/1 Jul 2022 dates so electronic monitoring is not engaged.
* B – 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 for electronic monitoring and, on a 25-employee reading, <25 for disconnect. The employer voluntarily maintains a disconnect policy since 2020 and an online-monitoring policy since late 2021 and refuses to distribute them to new hires on cost grounds. Colleagues split: the 25-employee threshold means no statutory duty to have/distribute, so a voluntary policy can be kept undistributed; others read the provision duty as attaching whenever a policy is held and the refusal to give the required disconnect policy to new employees is a statutory breach.
* C – ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, >25 on both reference dates. The employer says it has written and appropriately distributed both the disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring policies. The contentious point is the provision regime: policies are updated every month but a copy is only given to each employee every fiscal quarter. Several colleagues argue that is a failure to provide a revised policy as soon as practicable / within the statutory window for both s.43.1 and s.43.2 policies. Others treat quarterly re-issue as substantial compliance.
* D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and on 2 Jan 2023. The disconnect policy is written and appropriately distributed. No electronic-monitoring policy has ever been developed. On 1 Jan 2022 the employer was a 25+ employer so the electronic-monitoring duty attached on 1 Jan 2022 and, on 1 Jul 2022, the disconnecting duty attached. The post-March head-count falls below 25, so on a current-head-count reading the disconnect duty would no longer be mandatory and the electronic-monitoring duty would be out of scope on 2 Jan 2023. The dominant view in the room is that the 30-employee 1 Jan 2022 snapshot triggers a continuing obligation and the absence of a required electronic-monitoring policy is a historic and continuing non-compliance with the ESA as of 2 Jan 2023.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 Aug 2022, –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 bring head-count to 24. <25 on the reference dates and <20 on 2 Jan 2023, so no statutory disconnect/electronic-monitoring policy is required on the facts given.

The core disagreement is between the historic-trigger view for D – 30 on 1 Jan 2022 → electronic-monitoring policy never put in place → non-compliance as of 2 Jan 2023 – and the current-compliance views: B’s refusal to distribute a policy it voluntarily holds, and C’s monthly-update/quarterly-distribution practice as untimely provision of revised policies, and, with the 20-employee disconnect threshold effective 1 Jan 2023, A’s lack of a disconnect policy for 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The most repeated single answer in the round is D, the classic 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 employer lacking the required electronic-monitoring policy.
reflection_text.15:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA are the operative regime as of 2 Jan 2023.

* Electronic monitoring s.86 ESA – in force 1 Jan 2022. Applies to an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees. A written policy is required and must be given to employees.
* Disconnecting from work s.43.1 ESA – in force 2 Jun 2022, 25+ employees. A written policy is required and must be given to employees and a revised policy must be given on change.

Triggering is by the headcount at the statutory reference date. Once the 25-employee threshold is met on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring / on the June-July 2022 effective date for disconnecting, the obligation attaches for that employer-year and is not cured by a later fall below 25.

* A – 20 employees 1 Jan 2022 and 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023. Under a 25+ test no statutory disconnect/electronic monitoring duty is engaged on 2 Jan 2023. The 20+ extension that comes into force 1 Jan 2023 would make the 20-employee headcount a duty trigger and the absence of a disconnect policy would be a breach; that point is in dispute.
* B – 23 employees. <25 on both trigger dates, so no statutory duty to have a disconnect or electronic monitoring policy. The employer has voluntarily adopted both policies since 2020/2021. The refusal to distribute to new hires is a distribution problem. Under a strict 25+ statutory test the refusal does not create a statutory breach because the duties are not engaged; if the 20+ disconnect extension is applied, the employer is covered and the refusal to provide the required policy to new employees is a breach of the provision obligation.
* C – ~1,000 employees throughout 2022 >25 on all material dates. Written disconnect and electronic monitoring policies exist and are said to be appropriately distributed. The ongoing practice is monthly policy updates with a copy provided to each employee only every fiscal quarter. The ESA requires a copy of a revised policy to be provided to employees when the policy changes. The monthly-update/quarterly-distribution lag is the basis for a non-compliance argument on timeliness of provision of revised policies. Some colleagues treat the quarterly re-issue as substantively compliant.
* D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. The 25-employee threshold is therefore met on the electronic monitoring effective date and on the disconnect effective date. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy but has never developed an electronic monitoring policy. Headcount fell to 24 on 15 Mar 2022 and stays at 24 on 2 Jan 2023. The drop below 25 does not retroactively extinguish the obligation that attached on 1 Jan 2022. The absence of a required electronic monitoring policy for the period in which the employer was a 25+ employer is a continuing statutory breach as of 2 Jan 2023. If the obligation is assessed solely on current 2 Jan 2023 headcount, the employer is now <25 and the electronic monitoring duty would not be currently engaged, but the classic “once triggered” analysis treats D as the clear historic failure.
* E – 22 employees 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023, 24 only after the 15 Feb 2023 hires. <25 on both trigger dates and under a 25+ test no policy is required. Under a 20+ disconnect extension the employer is still <20 on 2 Jan 2023.

The dominant thread in the deliberation is the once-triggered electronic monitoring failure in D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 triggers the 1 Jan 2022 electronic monitoring duty and the employer has no electronic monitoring policy at all, while it does have a disconnect policy. That is the textbook non-compliance. The minority / alternative threads are:

* The 20+ disconnect extension effective 1 Jan 2023, which would make A with 20 employees and no policy, and B with 23 employees and a refusal to distribute, non-compliant on 2 Jan 2023.
* The timeliness of provision of revised policies in C, monthly updates with quarterly distribution, which some colleagues read as a failure to provide a revised policy contemporaneously with a change.

Unresolved: whether the analysis should apply the 20-employee disconnect threshold that came into force 1 Jan 2023 and, if so, whether the 3/6 month grace period applies to employers newly covered on 1 Jan 2023; and whether a quarterly provision of a monthly-updated policy satisfies the “provide the updated policy” obligation. The most consistently supported non-compliant employer under the conventional 25+ triggering analysis is D.
reflection_text.20:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA create two written-policy duties.

* Electronic monitoring – employers who regularly employ 25 or more employees, in force 1 Jan 2022. A written policy is required and must be provided to employees.
* Disconnecting from work – employers who regularly employ 25 or more employees, in force 2 Jun/1 Jul 2022. Working for Workers Act, 2022 lowers the disconnect threshold to 20 or more employees effective 1 Jan 2023, with a compliance window to 2 Jun 2023 for the 20-24 band.

Assessment is on the statutory reference headcount. Once the 25-employee threshold is met on the reference date the electronic monitoring obligation attaches for that year and the failure to put the policy in place is not cured by a later fall below 25. The disconnect obligation for 2023 is 20+.

A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 for electronic monitoring. For disconnect the 20+ threshold is met on 2 Jan 2023. No policy is in place. If the 20-24 grace to 2 Jun 2023 is applied the employer is within the compliance window; on a strict in-force reading it would be non-compliant.

B – 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 for electronic monitoring, 20+ for disconnect. A written disconnect policy exists since 2020 and a voluntary online-monitoring policy exists since late 2021. The ESA distribution duty attaches to a required policy. Refusal to distribute a voluntarily maintained policy on cost grounds is the contested point; the disconnect policy is required in the 20+ band and must be provided to employees, including new hires.

C – ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, >25 on all material dates. Both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic monitoring policy are written and “appropriately distributed”. The employer updates both policies monthly but supplies a copy to each employee only every fiscal quarter. The ESA requires a copy of the policy and a copy of any new or revised policy to be provided to employees. Monthly change / quarterly provision is the basis for a timing / “as soon as practicable” argument that the employer is not providing updated policies contemporaneously with change.

D – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and on 2 Jan 2023. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy is in place; no electronic monitoring policy has ever been developed. On 1 Jan 2022 the employer was a 25+ employer, so the electronic monitoring duty was triggered for 2022. The subsequent reduction to 24 does not retroactively extinguish the 2022 obligation and the policy remains absent on 2 Jan 2023. On a current-headcount reading the employer is now <25 for electronic monitoring and 24 ≥20 for disconnect, so it would appear compliant on current headcount.

E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 resignations Aug 2022, –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 = 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 take the shop to 24. <25 for electronic monitoring and <20 for disconnect on 2 Jan 2023, no policy required as of the assessment date.

The majority view in the round is D as the historic electronic-monitoring non-compliance triggered by the 30-employee 1 Jan 2022 headcount and never remedied. The competing arguments are C’s monthly update / quarterly provision practice as a breach of the provide-on-change duty, and B’s refusal to distribute voluntarily maintained policies to new hires. The 20+ disconnect phase-in and grace period to 2 Jun 2023 is the unresolved timing issue that affects A and B.

The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA create two written-policy duties that are head-count triggered on a reference date and that must be in writing and provided to employees.

* Electronic monitoring policy – s.78.1 ff. In force 1 January 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees.
* Disconnecting from work policy – s.43.1 ff. In force 1 July 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees.

The duty is determined by the size of the employer on the statutory reference date. Once the 25-employee threshold is met on that date the employer is required to have the written policy in place on the effective date and to provide it to its employees. A later reduction in headcount does not retroactively cure a failure to have the policy in place when the obligation first attached.

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements that start 10 Jan 2023 will only take the employer to 28 after the start date. <25 on both trigger dates, no electronic monitoring or disconnecting policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. Compliant.

B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both the 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022 reference dates so neither a disconnecting-from-work nor an electronic-monitoring policy is statutorily required. The policies it has are voluntary and the ESA does not impose a statutory distribution duty where the size threshold is not met.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. The employer is well above 25 on both trigger dates and the fact pattern states it has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy. The ESA requires a copy of the policy to be provided to employees and a copy of any new or revised policy to be provided when the policy changes. Updating the policies monthly and circulating the current version to the workforce on a quarterly cycle is an operational implementation of that provision duty for a 1,000-person employer. The facts expressly describe the policies as appropriately distributed and the quarterly circulation of a consolidated update satisfies the “provide the updated policy” obligation in substance. There is no statutory 30-day clock quoted on the facts and a quarterly provision of the current version is a reasonable compliance approach.

E. 22 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 20 after the August resignations, 18 on 2 Jan 2023 after the 31 Dec retirements. The 6 hires on 15 Feb 2023 bring the employer to 24. <25 on all relevant dates, no disconnecting or electronic monitoring policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. Compliant.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. The 25-employee threshold was therefore met on the reference date for the electronic monitoring obligation that was in force 1 January 2022, and for the disconnecting-from-work obligation that was in force 1 July 2022. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, which is fine, but it has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring at all.

The 6 dismissals on 15 March 2022 reduced headcount to 24 and it remained at 24 through the remainder of 2022. That subsequent drop does not remove the requirement that attached when the employer was a 30-employee employer on 1 January 2022. The failure to have a written electronic monitoring policy in place when the obligation arose is a continuing non-compliance with the ESA as of 2 January 2023, whereas the missing distribution timing issue raised for C is debatable and the fact pattern itself characterizes C’s distribution as appropriate.

On a strict trigger-date analysis D is the clear statutory gap: a covered employer with no electronic monitoring policy.

D is the employer that is not in compliance as of 2 January 2023.

The Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA create two written-policy duties that are head-count triggered on a reference date and that must be in writing and provided to employees.

* Electronic monitoring policy – s.78.1 ff. In force 1 January 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees.
* Disconnecting from work policy – s.43.1 ff. In force 1 July 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees.

The duty is determined by the size of the employer on the statutory reference date. Once the 25-employee threshold is met on that date the employer is required to have the written policy in place on the effective date and to provide it to its employees. A later reduction in headcount does not retroactively cure a failure to have the policy in place when the obligation first attached.

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements that start 10 Jan 2023 will only take the employer to 28 after the start date. <25 on both trigger dates, no electronic monitoring or disconnecting policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. Compliant.

B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both the 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022 reference dates so neither a disconnecting-from-work nor an electronic-monitoring policy is statutorily required. The policies it has are voluntary and the ESA does not impose a statutory distribution duty where the size threshold is not met.

C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. The employer is well above 25 on both trigger dates and the fact pattern states it has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy. The ESA requires a copy of the policy to be provided to employees and a copy of any new or revised policy to be provided when the policy changes. Updating the policies monthly and circulating the current version to the workforce on a quarterly cycle is an operational implementation of that provision duty for a 1,000-person employer. The facts expressly describe the policies as appropriately distributed and the quarterly circulation of a consolidated update satisfies the “provide the updated policy” obligation in substance. There is no statutory 30-day clock quoted on the facts and a quarterly provision of the current version is a reasonable compliance approach.

E. 22 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 20 after the August resignations, 18 on 2 Jan 2023 after the 31 Dec retirements. The 6 hires on 15 Feb 2023 bring the employer to 24. <25 on all relevant dates, no disconnecting or electronic monitoring policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. Compliant.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. The 25-employee threshold was therefore met on the reference date for the electronic monitoring obligation that was in force 1 January 2022, and for the disconnecting-from-work obligation that was in force 1 July 2022. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, which is fine, but it has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring at all.

The 6 dismissals on 15 March 2022 reduced headcount to 24 and it remained at 24 through the remainder of 2022. That subsequent drop does not remove the requirement that attached when the employer was a 30-employee employer on 1 January 2022. The failure to have a written electronic monitoring policy in place when the obligation arose is a continuing non-compliance with the ESA as of 2 January 2023, whereas the missing distribution timing issue raised for C is debatable and the fact pattern itself characterizes C’s distribution as appropriate.

On a strict trigger-date analysis D is the clear statutory gap: a covered employer with no electronic monitoring policy.

D

On 1 Jan 2022 the electronic monitoring policy duty under the Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA came into force for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees. The disconnecting from work duty came into force for 25+ employers on 1 July 2022.

The headcount test is made at the statutory reference date. Once the 25-employee threshold is met on that date the employer is in scope for the year and is required to have a written policy in place and to provide it to employees. A later reduction below 25 does not retroactively cure a failure that existed when the obligation first attached.

* A – 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates. No disconnecting or electronic monitoring policy is required yet.
* B – 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates, so neither duty is statutorily required. The employer may voluntarily maintain policies; a refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not a statutory breach under the ESA.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 after August resignations, 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements = 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 6 hires on 15 Feb 2023 take the shop to 24. <25 on the relevant dates, no policy required on 2 Jan 2023.
* C – ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. It is clearly a 25+ employer. The facts state it has written and appropriately distributed both a disconnecting from work policy and an electronic monitoring policy. Updating the policies monthly as internal housekeeping and re-issuing the current version each fiscal quarter is a reasonable way of keeping employees informed and satisfies the provide-on-change obligation. There is no present-day substantive or distribution failure on the facts given.

D is the clear non-compliance. The employer employed 30 individuals on 1 Jan 2022, so the electronic monitoring obligation was triggered on that date and a written electronic monitoring policy was required to be in place and provided to employees. It has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting from work policy, but it has not developed an electronic monitoring policy at all.

The 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 reduce headcount to 24 thereafter and take the employer below the 25-employee threshold for the remainder of 2022. That reduction does not remove the duty that properly attached on 1 Jan 2022 when the employer was a 30-employee employer, and the missing electronic monitoring policy is still absent on 2 Jan 2023. That is a statutory breach of the electronic monitoring policy regime.

On the classic trigger-date analysis, D is the employer that is not in compliance with applicable employment laws in Ontario as of 2 January 2023.

D

Electronic monitoring under s.43.2 ESA came into force 1 January 2022 for employers who regularly employ 25 or more employees. Disconnecting from work under s.43.1 ESA came into force 1 July 2022, also for 25+ employers. The obligation attaches on the basis of the size of the employer at the statutory reference date and, once attached, the employer must have a written policy in place and make it available to the employees.

* A: 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023. No 25+ threshold is met on either trigger date, so no mandatory disconnecting or electronic monitoring policy is required as of 2 Jan 2023.
* B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates. The disconnecting and electronic monitoring duties are not statutorily engaged. The employer may maintain voluntary policies; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy does not create an ESA breach.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022, minus 2 resignations and minus 2 retirements = 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 brings the employer to 24. <25 on the material dates, no mandatory policy is required.
* C: ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, well above 25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. The facts state the employer has written and appropriately distributed both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic monitoring policy. The monthly internal update with quarterly issuance of the current version is a reasonable way of keeping the workforce advised of the policy that is in force; the question expressly tells us the policies are written and appropriately distributed.

* D: 30 individuals on 1 Jan 2022. The 25-employee threshold was therefore met on the statutory reference date for electronic monitoring and for disconnecting from work. That triggers the obligation to have a written electronic monitoring policy in place by the effective date and to provide it to employees. The employer does have a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, but it has “not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all.

The subsequent termination of 6 employees on 15 Mar 2022, bringing headcount to 24 for the remainder of 2022, does not retroactively extinguish an obligation that properly attached on 1 Jan 2022 when the employer was a 30-employee employer. The electronic monitoring duty was triggered by the 1 Jan 2022 complement and remains unremedied as of 2 Jan 2023. That is a clear statutory non-compliance for an employer who was in scope on the trigger date, whereas the other employers are either below the threshold or are described as having the required written and appropriately distributed policies.

On the classic Working for Workers trigger analysis, employer D is the one that is not in compliance.

D

The Working for Workers Act, 2021 added two written-policy duties under the ESA.

* Electronic monitoring: in force 1 Jan 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees.
* Disconnecting from work: in force 2 June 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees, phase-in to 20+ from 1 Jan 2023.

The duty is triggered by the size of the employer on the statutory reference date. Once the 25-employee threshold is met on that date the employer is required to have a written policy in place and to give it to employees. The obligation that attaches on the trigger date is not cured by a later fall in headcount.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 Jan 2022. That is the reference date for the electronic monitoring obligation which came into force 1 Jan 2022. A written electronic monitoring policy was therefore required for that employer for the 2022 calendar year and the policy was required to be provided to the workforce.

The facts say the employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, but it has “not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all. The six terminations on 15 Mar 2022 bring headcount to 24 thereafter, and the employer is at 24 on 2 Jan 2023, so the disconnecting-from-work duty is not currently engaged for 2023 and the disconnect policy the employer holds is supererogatory. The later reduction does not retroactively remove the electronic monitoring requirement that attached on 1 Jan 2022 when the employer was a 30-employee employer. The employer was in scope when the law came into force and it never put the required electronic monitoring policy in place. That is a continuing failure as of 2 Jan 2023.

A, B and E are all below the 25-employee threshold on the relevant reference dates and are therefore not presently required to have the statutory policies. A’s 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023, E’s 6 hires start 15 Feb 2023 and will leave it at 24, and B is at 23 with only voluntary policies.

C is above 25 throughout 2022 and does have both a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic monitoring policy that are written and appropriately distributed in the first instance. Updating the policies every month and then providing a copy of the current version to each employee every fiscal quarter is a reasonable method of keeping employees informed of the policy. The ESA requires a written policy and that employees be given a copy and be given a copy of any revised policy. It does not prescribe an immediate same-day handout for every monthly tweak, and quarterly distribution of the current, up-to-date policy satisfies the provide-and-make-available duty in practice. On the facts given C is a covered employer that is substantively in compliance.

The clear statutory failure on the facts as of 2 Jan 2023 is D’s absence of the electronic monitoring policy that was required when the employer was a 25+ employer on 1 Jan 2022 and which was never developed.

D is different. The employer employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That is the reference date for the electronic monitoring obligation that came into force 1 January 2022. On the trigger date analysis under the Working for Workers Act, 2021 the only clear statutory failure on 2 January 2023 is D.

Electronic monitoring and disconnecting from work are both threshold policies under the ESA. Electronic monitoring is in force 1 January 2022 for employers who regularly employ 25 or more employees; disconnecting from work is in force 1 July 2022 for employers who regularly employ 25 or more employees. The test is the headcount on the statutory reference date for the year and, once the threshold is met on that date, the employer must have a written policy in place and must provide it to employees. A later fall below 25 does not retroactively erase the obligation that attached when the threshold was met.

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on the relevant dates. No mandatory disconnecting or electronic monitoring policy is required yet. The 3/6 month grace period only runs from 10 Jan 2023.

B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 employees so neither the disconnecting from work nor the electronic monitoring duty is statutorily engaged. The employer has voluntary policies in place since 2020/2021. Where a policy is voluntary, a refusal to distribute it is not a breach of the ESA provision and distribution duties. The cost refusal argument does not create a statutory breach for a <25 employer.

C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022. The employer is clearly in scope and it does have written disconnecting from work and electronic monitoring policies that are written and have been appropriately distributed in the first instance. The ESA requires a copy of the policy to be provided to employees and a copy of any revised policy to be provided when the policy changes. Updating the policies internally every month and circulating the current version to the workforce each fiscal quarter is a reasonable, contemporaneous way of keeping employees informed of the policy that is in effect at any given time. Quarterly provision of the current, up to date policy satisfies the provision and change-notification obligation in substance; there is no requirement for a per-change push within a few weeks where the workforce is regularly being given the current version and can request the policy at any time. On the facts there is no evidence the employer is withholding the policy or failing to make it available.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. The 25-employee threshold was therefore met on the statutory reference date for electronic monitoring in force 1 Jan 2022 and for disconnecting from work in force 1 July 2022. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting from work policy, so that part of the obligation is met. It has not developed an electronic monitoring policy at all. The 6 terminations on 15 Mar 2022 reduce headcount to 24 for the remainder of 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. A subsequent drop below 25 does not cure the failure to have a required electronic monitoring policy in place for the period in which the employer was a 25+ employer, and the policy remains absent on 2 Jan 2023. That is a continuing non-compliance with the electronic monitoring policy requirement that attached on 1 Jan 2022.

E. 22 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 20 after August resignations, 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements, 24 after the 15 Feb 2023 hires. <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and was never 25+ on the relevant reference dates. No mandatory disconnecting or electronic monitoring policy is required on the assessment date.

That leaves D as the employer that was captured by the 1 Jan 2022 25+ trigger and that never put a required electronic monitoring policy in place.

An employer who is 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 must have a written electronic monitoring policy in place on that date and must give it to its employees. The obligation is acquired by the 1 Jan 2022 size test.
* Disconnecting from work – ESA s.43.1 et seq., in force 1 Jul 2022 for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees, with the same reference-date logic.

Current headcount on 2 Jan 2023 matters only for a new threshold crossing, not for curing a failure that was acquired on the 1 Jan 2022 reference date.

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates, no mandatory policy is required on 2 Jan 2023. A 3/6 month grace period will only run from 10 Jan 2023.

B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both trigger dates so neither a disconnecting-from-work nor an electronic-monitoring policy is statutorily required. C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. The employer is unequivocally covered. The facts state the employer has written and appropriately distributed both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic-monitoring policy. The monthly internal update with quarterly circulation of the current version is how the employer keeps the workforce informed. The “appropriately distributed” description in the facts is the ESA test of having given the policy to employees and making revisions available in the normal course of business. A quarterly provision of the then-current policy is a reasonable implementation of the duty to provide the policy and any changes; it does not make the employer non-compliant on 2 Jan 2023.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022. The electronic-monitoring obligation therefore attached on 1 Jan 2022 and the disconnecting-from-work obligation attached on the 1 Jul 2022 reference date. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, satisfying that part.

An obligation that attached on the reference date is not cured by a later fall below 25, and the policy remains absent on 2 Jan 2023.

That is a continuing statutory breach for an employer who was 25+ on the 1 Jan 2022 trigger date and never put the required electronic-monitoring policy in place. D is the employer that is not in compliance as of 2 January 2023.

D

The electronic monitoring and disconnecting-from-work duties under the Working for Workers Act, 2021 are size triggered and the trigger is made on the statutory reference date for the year in question.

* Electronic monitoring – ESA s.78.1ff, in force 1 Jan 2022 for an employer who normally employs 25 or more employees. An employer who is 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 is an employer to whom the duty applies for that year and the written policy must be in place and provided to employees on the effective date.
* Disconnecting from work – ESA s.43.1ff, in force 1 Jul 2022 for an employer who normally employs 25 or more employees.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 Jan 2022. On that reference date the employer is an employer who normally employs 25 or more employees and the electronic monitoring duty therefore attached on 1 Jan 2022. 

The employer does have a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy. It has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. The 6 terminations on 15 Mar 2022 reduced the headcount to 24 thereafter and to 24 on 2 Jan 2023, but that subsequent reduction does not retroactively extinguish an obligation that properly attached on the 1 Jan 2022 reference date. The electronic monitoring policy that was required to be in place when the employer was a 30-employee employer on 1 Jan 2022 is still absent on 2 Jan 2023.

The other choices do not present a clear statutory breach on the facts as assessed on 2 Jan 2023 on a 25+ trigger basis:

* A is 20 on 2 Jan 2023 and <25 on the 1 Jan 2022 electronic-monitoring / disconnect reference dates. The 8 hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023.
* B is 23 on the assessment date, <25, so no statutory disconnect/electronic monitoring duty is engaged; any voluntary policies are not statutorily enforceable.
* C is >25 throughout 2022 and does have written and distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies in place.
* E is 18 on 2 Jan 2023, <25 on the relevant 1 Jan 2022 / 1 Jul 2022 reference dates.

The historic failure to ever put a required electronic monitoring policy in place for the period in which D was a 25+ employer is a continuing non-compliance with the ESA as of 2 Jan 2023.

* Electronic / online monitoring – ESA s.86.1 ff. 25+ employees, in force 1 Jan 2022.  A written policy must be in place and provided to employees when the 25+ threshold is met and on any change.
* Right to disconnect – ESA s.43.1 ff. 25+ employees, in force 2 Jun 2022, and the size threshold for the disconnect duty was reduced to 20+ employees with effect 1 Jan 2023. A written policy must be in place and provided to employees when the 20+ threshold is met and on any change.

Assessed on the headcount that exists on 2 Jan 2023:

C

As of 2 January 2023 a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy are mandatory for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees.

* Disconnecting from work – ESA s.43.1 ff. In force 2 June 2022 for 25+; the Working for Workers Act 2022 lowers the disconnect threshold to 20+ with effect 1 January 2023. Employers who are in the 20-24 band on 1 January 2023 are given a transitional compliance window to 1 June/July 2023.  The transition means that on 2 January 2023 the mandatory disconnect duty that is immediately enforceable is still the 25+ duty.
* Electronic monitoring – ESA s.78.1 ff. In force 1 January 2022 for 25+ employees.

Applied to the fact patterns:

A. 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The employer is <25 and is in the 20-24 transitional band for disconnect. No disconnect or e-m policy is mandatorily required on the assessment date. The 8 hires that start 10 January 2023 only start the future grace clock.

B. 23 employees on the assessment date. <25 so the mandatory disconnect/e-m duties are not immediately enforceable and the employer is in the 20-24 transitional band for disconnect. The written policies it holds are voluntary. The refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not a statutory breach of the ESA on 2 January 2023.

D. 30 employees on 1 January 2022 → 6 terminations 15 March 2022 → 24 employees thereafter and on 2 January 2023. On a current headcount basis the employer is <25 on 2 January 2023. It has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy. A written electronic monitoring policy is not required for an employer who employs <25 employees on the assessment date. The historic 1 January 2022 trigger does not keep an e-m obligation alive once the employer is no longer a 25+ employer on the relevant date.

E. 22 → 20 → 18 employees on 2 January 2023. 18 employees on the assessment date and 24 only after the 15 February 2023 hires. <25 and in the <20 disconnect band on 2 January 2023. No mandatory policy is required on the assessment date.

C is in scope and in breach of the provision/distribution duties. The employer regularly employs ≈1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 at all times, i.e. >25 on all material dates. It is therefore statutorily required to have both a written disconnecting-from-work policy and a written electronic-monitoring policy and to give each employee a copy of the policy and a copy of any new or revised policy when the policy is changed.

The ESA requires the updated policy to be provided to employees when the policy is changed, not up to a quarter later. Updating the two required policies every month but only providing a copy of the updated policies to each employee every fiscal quarter means employees can be working for up to ~60-90 days under a version of the policy that the employer has already superseded. That is a failure to provide a copy of a revised policy “when the policy is changed” for both the disconnecting-from-work policy and the electronic-monitoring policy.

C is the only employer that is statutorily required to have the policies on the assessment date and is failing to meet the ongoing provision/notice requirement.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 creates two written-policy duties under the ESA for employers who regularly employ 25 or more employees: electronic monitoring in force 1 Jan 2022; disconnecting from work in force 2 Jun/1 Jul 2022 for 25+. The Working for Workers Act, 2022 lowers the disconnect threshold to 20+ with effect 1 Jan 2023, with a dispute in the room about whether the 20-24 band is immediately enforceable on 2 Jan 2023 or has a transitional compliance window to ~1 Jun/July 2023.

Trigger mechanics remain contested:

* Historic-trigger view: the size test is made on the statutory reference date, 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring and 1 Jul 2022 for disconnect 25+. Once triggered the duty is not cured by a later fall below 25. That view makes D a clear breach: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 → electronic monitoring duty attached 1 Jan 2022; employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy but “has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all. The 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter does not retroactively remove the 1 Jan 2022 trigger. D is the most repeated single answer in the round under this reading.

* Current-headcount view: duties are assessed on the headcount that exists on 2 Jan 2023, with the 20+ disconnect phase-in applied. That view makes A the clearest current breach: 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023, no disconnect policy, and 20≥20 from 1 Jan 2023. The 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023 do not change the 2 Jan 2023 complement. Colleagues 10,11,12 argue A is non-compliant with s.43.1 on the 20+ threshold; colleague 1 argues the 20+ duty is not immediately enforceable on 2 Jan 2023 and the transitional window applies. B at 23 employees is in the 20+ band and does have a written disconnect policy since 2020, but refuses to distribute it to new hires on cost grounds. Some colleagues treat the refusal as a distribution breach once the 20+ duty is engaged; others treat B’s policies as voluntary because <25 on the original 25+ test and the refusal is not a statutory breach.

C: ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, >25 on all material dates. Facts state written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. The dispute is provision timing: policies are updated monthly but a copy is only given to each employee every fiscal quarter. Colleague 1/3/20 argue quarterly issuance is too late under “provide when changed / as soon as practicable”. Colleagues 13,14,15,16,17,18,19,21 argue the facts explicitly say “appropriately distributed” and quarterly circulation of the current version is substantively compliant; no 30-day clock is stated.

B distribution debate: 23 employees <25 for the original 25+ duties. Some say no statutory duty to have/distribute, so refusal to distribute voluntary policies is not a breach. Others, with the 20+ phase-in, say a disconnect policy is now required and must be provided to new hires; refusal is a breach.

E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug → –2 31 Dec = 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <20 on 2 Jan 2023, <25 for electronic monitoring. No statutory duty on assessment date under either reading.

Remaining disagreements:
- Whether the 20+ disconnect duty is immediately enforceable 1 Jan 2023 or subject to a grace window to mid-2023.
- Whether D’s electronic monitoring obligation persists after headcount fell to 24, or is assessed on current headcount.
- Whether C’s monthly-update/quarterly-distribution practice is a failure to provide a revised policy on change.
- Whether B’s cost-based refusal to distribute a policy it voluntarily holds is a statutory breach when the employer is <25 for the 25+ duties but possibly ≥20 for the new disconnect duty.

My current understanding: D is the classic historic-trigger non-compliance for lacking an electronic monitoring policy after being 30 strong on 1 Jan 2022. A is a strong contender under a strict current 20+ immediate-enforcement reading, and C’s quarterly distribution is the provision-timing argument that keeps appearing. The room is split between historic-trigger D and current 20+ A, with C as a minority provision-timing view.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA duties in play:

* Electronic monitoring – s.78.1 ff, 25+ employees, in force 1 Jan 2022 for employers 25+ on the 1 Jan 2022 reference date. Written policy + provide to employees.
* Disconnecting from work – s.43.1 ff, 25+ employees, in force 2 Jun / 1 Jul 2022 for employers 25+ on the 1 Jul 2022 reference date. Working for Workers Act 2022 lowers the disconnect threshold to 20+ with effect 1 Jan 2023. Colleagues split on whether the 20-24 band is immediate on 1 Jan 2023 or has a transitional compliance window to ~1 Jun/Jul 2023.

Headcounts on 2 Jan 2023:
A. 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023 → 28. No electronic monitoring duty. Disconnect duty under 20+ is engaged if immediate; no policy exists.
B. 23 employees. No 25+ electronic monitoring duty. Disconnect duty under 20+ is engaged if immediate; employer does have a written disconnect policy since 2020 and a voluntary online monitoring policy since late 2021, but refuses to distribute to new hires on cost grounds.
C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012. >25 on all material dates. Written and “appropriately distributed” disconnect and electronic monitoring policies per facts. Updates policies monthly but provides copy to each employee only every fiscal quarter. Dispute is whether monthly-change/quarterly-distribution violates the provide-on-change obligation.
D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter and on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed. Historic 25+ trigger on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring. Dispute is whether the duty is permanently locked by the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot or ceases once headcount falls below 25. Most colleagues treat the 1 Jan 2022 trigger as locking in the electronic monitoring duty for 2022 and holding that the subsequent drop to 24 does not cure the historic failure; the missing electronic monitoring policy is a continuing breach as of 2 Jan 2023. If assessed purely on current headcount on 2 Jan 2023, employer is 24 ≥20 for disconnect but <25 for electronic monitoring, and the disconnect policy it holds would be sufficient.
E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug resignations → 18 after 31 Dec retirements. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023, 24 after 15 Feb 2023 hires. <25 for electronic monitoring; <20 for disconnect on 2 Jan 2023, so no statutory policy duty engaged on assessment date under current-headcount reading.

Competing interpretations emerging in round 1:

* Historic trigger camp: D is the clear breach – 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 triggered electronic monitoring, policy never developed, and a later fall below 25 does not retroactively cure the 2022 requirement. This was the consensus in round 0 and is still held by a large minority in round 1. C’s quarterly distribution is read as substantively compliant because the facts expressly say “appropriately distributed”; the monthly update issue is debatable.

* Current-headcount 20+ immediate camp: On 1 Jan 2023 the disconnect threshold is 20+. A has 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023 with no disconnect policy → breach. B has 23 employees, in scope for disconnect, and refusal to distribute to new hires is a distribution breach. D on current headcount is 24 employees, so disconnect duty is met by the existing policy and electronic monitoring is not required <25. This view treats the 20+ duty as immediately enforceable on 2 Jan 2023 and treats the electronic monitoring duty as not persisting after headcount drops below 25.

* Distribution-timing camp: C is non-compliant because updating monthly but only providing a copy quarterly means employees work under superseded policy for up to ~2-3 months, failing the provide-on-change obligation.
